HEADLINE: Afterpay takes aim at Wall Street
TEXT:
Is buy now, pay later giant Afterpay outgrowing its Australian roots?

That is the strong impression given by the group's announcement yesterday that it will spend up to $595 million to increase its ownership in Afterpay US, from 80 per cent up to 93 per cent, by buying shares in the US operation from major investor Matrix Partners and American employees.

The Matrix transaction values the US operation at just 28 per cent of Afterpay's $38 billion market capitalisation, or $10.6 billion. That's either good news or bad news for Afterpay's ASX investors, depending on whether you think the entire group is overvalued.

If you're an Afterpay believer, then the Matrix price looks to be a bargain, given the US now accounts for 43 per cent of underlying sales, and rising fast. Sales in North America soared 195 per cent in the December half to $4.2 billion, easily outstripping the 53 per cent growth in Australian underlying sales, which hit $4.8 billion.

Of course, the alternative view is that Matrix would have driven a hard bargain and this is proof the US business is worth less than was implied by Afterpay's soaring share price.

There may also be some disquiet among investors who might see the $225 million that Afterpay could end up paying to employee share scheme participants under this deal as effectively representing staff costs that should have gone through the group's profit and loss statement.

Founders and co-chief executives Nick Molnar and Anthony Eisen insist the deal is highly earnings accretive and argue it will help simplify the ownership of Afterpay US and, more importantly, align it with the way Afterpay is internally organised now - that is, not on regional lines, but around global functions.

But it is also important to note that mopping up Matrix and US staff with stock in the US division would also make it easier for Afterpay to potentially tap what it says is growing demand from US-based investors by listing in the US.

Like every buy now, pay later investor in the world, Eisen and Molnar watched as US-based Affirm listed on the Nasdaq in January at $US49 a share and surged to $US140 before drifting back in recent weeks to close at $102.49 overnight Wednesday.

But to grab a slice of the clear US interest in buy now, pay later, a cleaner ownership structure for the US business is vital.

Eisen says the Afterpay register is already shifting to include more US institutions, and while he emphasises there is no timeline for a listing outside Australia, the company was keen to show it is on the board's radar.

"If it's in shareholders' best interests to consider an additional listing, the board [is] in tune with that."

A more globally focused outlook will also be important and the groundwork for a potential pitch to US investors was noticeable in the presentation Eisen and Molnar delivered to investors yesterday at it announced its December-half results.

Yes, the big numbers got a run - total underlying sales up 106 per cent to $9.8 billion, active customers up 80 per cent to 13.1 million, active merchants up 73 per cent to 74,700 and underlying earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation up more than six-fold to $47.9 million.

The 30 basis point improvement in gross losses as a percentage of underlying sales, which fell from 1 per cent to 0.7 per cent, was also impressive.

And yes, there was a plenty of other titbits in the result to watch, including a $1.3 billion capital raising to help pay for the Matrix deal and a sell-down by Eisen and Molnar of up to $60 million each.

But there was also a distinct emphasis on how Afterpay is different to the increasingly crowded market that it plays in.

The key argument here is that Afterpay has built a level of customer loyalty that is very different to its competitors. Fast growth in active customers is important, but Eisen and Molnar argue that more important is the fact that the longer a customer is on the platform, the more regularly they use it.

In Afterpay's most mature market, Australia, for example, customers who have been on the platform for more than four years use the platform an average of 29.1 times a year. Users who have been on it for three years use it 20.7 times a year, and users who have been on for less than a year transact an average of 3.9 times.

These trends are similar in the US and Britain. Afterpay says this is different to its competitors, whose customers tend to spend strongly in their first month but then fade quickly.

"It really is the power of our platform that is fuelling not only our growth, but that we see as an emerging differentiation in the market," says Eisen.

He also points out that while repeat usage improves the longer a customer is on the platform, the other benefit of increased tenure and frequency is lower loss rates.

On the other side of the platform, Eisen also argues that Afterpay is delivering for merchants.

First, every customer who joins the platform tends to spend widely; the top 10 per cent of customers across the global business spend an average of 31 times per year across an average of six industry verticals and 14 merchants.

Second, the Afterpay platform itself is delivering leads to retailers; for the first time yesterday, Afterpay revealed that 17 per cent of underlying sales were generated from users who came on to the Afterpay app or website first, and were then directed to a retailer.

Finally, Afterpay customers who start online are increasingly also shopping in a retailer's physical store and these omni-channel users tend to be the most valuable.

While an in-store-only user transacts an average of four times per year and an online-only user 11 times, omni-channel users transact an average of 26 times a year, 19 times online and seven in-store.

While growth in each of its individual markets amplifies these platform effects, Eisen and Molnar's bigger growth opportunities lie in pushing into new global markets - Europe is next and then Asia - and adding more products to the platform.

The first of these, called Afterpay Money, will formally launch in Australia in the September quarter of next year.

It will allow users to set up a transactional account, a debit and a digital wallet for payments (all powered by Westpac's 10X banking-as-a-service platform), create savings goals and see Afterpay transactions.

As Morgan Stanley commented last week, this product is unlikely to be much of a money spinner for Afterpay - deposit rates are simply too low to generate much revenue. What it will generate is more and more user data, which will allow the group to plot its next product expansion.

The debate around Afterpay's valuation is justified, but it tends to overshadow what Eisen and Molnar have created.

The network effects of this platform become more visible with every earnings result.

The loyalty of users is such that a strong growth in active customers results in even stronger growth in sales thanks to repeat transactions - which in turn pushes down loss rates and further improves returns.

Execution remains the pair's enduring challenge - juggling big growth in the US and Britain while pushing into Europe and Asia would test the limits of any organisation's management capacity, let alone a business less than seven years old - but Afterpay's latest numbers suggest they're pulling it off.

They'll need to keep doing that if they are to test themselves in the wilds of Wall Street.

HEADLINE: A2 Milk finds its daigou trade has curdled
TEXT:
Once upon a time - well, three or four years ago - companies like a2 Milk and Blackmores found themselves carried to ASX glory by a powerful and mysterious force called the daigou.

These mini entrepreneurs had developed a lucrative business model whereby they would buy popular wellness products from the shelves of Australian supermarkets and chemists - mainly baby formula and vitamins - and sell them to customers in mainland China, either directly or via Chinese e-commerce platforms.

If a2 and Blackmores could keep the shelves full - which wasn't easy given the extraordinary demand seen at times through the daigou channel - then they could watch the money roll in.

How times change. Having posted a 16 per cent fall in revenue for the December half to $NZ677.4 million ($632 million) and a 35 per cent fall in net profit to $120 million, a2 Milk is now offering what it describes as "temporary support to daigou-resellers" to help revive this sales channel.

It is understood that support will take the form of joint funding for promotions and customer recruitment.

There are a few factors that made life hard for the daigou. One is COVID-19, which of course has crippled tourism from China and hit international student numbers.

Another would appear to be customer demand back in China; online pricing has been subdued, so daigou have been slow to re-enter the market and promote the a2 brand, the company says.

The other factor is a2 building its China-label brand, which sells through retail stores in China. China label sales rose 45.2 per cent in the December half, with a2's market share increasing by 70 basis points to 2.4 per cent at the end of December.

a2 isn't giving up on the daigou trade. It sees the channel as strategically important, particularly for getting Chinese consumers hooked on the higher margin English-label product in what is an increasingly competitive market.

But while international borders remain closed, lifting demand through this channel will take time, as yesterday's earnings guidance downgrade for the full year makes clear.

Flight Centre rides COVID-19 in more ways than one: The pandemic giveth, and the pandemic taketh away. No one knows that better than Flight Centre boss Graeme Turner, who yesterday delivered a $247 million loss for the December half, as total transaction value fell to $1.5 billion, or just 12 per cent of what it was a year earlier.

But there was one little bright spot for Flight Centre. Its investment in 99Bikes, a chain of bike shops run by Turner's son, is doing very nicely as the nation spends more time at home and less time on public transport.

The chain's sales doubled in the first half as profit soared to $25 million, up from $5 million a year ago.

It hardly fills the pandemic-sized hole in Turner's profit and loss statement, but you've got to take what you can get in these tough times.

Turner made a strong argument yesterday that Flight Centre can emerge from the crisis a leaner business with a cost base, he says, is 66 per cent lower than a year ago, representing $1.9 billion in annual savings.

The company's cash burn during the period fell to $30 million a month (from about $41 million a month in the early stages of the pandemic), which should put it in a position to break even once the vaccine keeps domestic borders open permanently for leisure and business travel, and allows a limited amount of low-risk international travel.

Of course, who knows what that might mean for bike sales?

Life360 tracks potential bidders: Nothing like a little takeover talk to send your shares flying.

Shares in Life360, which makes an app that lets parents track the movements of their kids (and others), soared 22 per cent yesterday after the company casually mentioned at the bottom of its earnings release that, "given current valuations in the US for high-growth technology companies" it "has received inbound interest" that could result in a listing in the US, the sale of part of its business or a merger with a larger company.

A strategic review is under way to look at these and other options, including sticking with its existing growth plans, which delivered 39 per cent revenue growth in calendar 2020, despite a 2 per cent fall in global monthly average users.

The company posted an underlying loss of $US7.3 million ($9.2 million), a 68 per cent improvement on the prior year.

The San Francisco-based group has been hit by COVID-19, which keeps kids and their parents at home, but chief executive and co-founder Chris Hulls is confident that signs of recovery in January can set the company up for a good second half of 2021, when the US should be able to have a more normal "back to school" period as the vaccine rollout continues.

The big question is whether Life360 will exist in its current form by then.

HEADLINE: Ark ups Tesla bet despite record outflow
TEXT:
The largest outflow on record for Cathie Wood's Ark fund was not enough to stop the firm from increasing its bet on Tesla after the electric carmaker's stock closed below $US700 for the first time this year on Tuesday (Wednesday AEDT).

Wood, whose $US26.6 billion Ark Innovation exchange-traded fund was the top-performing actively managed US equity fund tracked by Morningstar last year, bought $US171 million of Tesla shares, pushing its weight to about 10 per cent of the fund.

Shares of the carmaker jumped 4.7 per cent in afternoon trading on Wednesday, helping erase some of the steep losses Ark has suffered over the last week as momentum stocks have pulled back sharply.

The sell-off triggered heavy trading, with $US5 billion of Ark Innovation shares changing hands on Tuesday - more than double the previous session's volume. The fund dipped slightly on Wednesday, pushing its loss to nearly 9 per cent for the week to date.

Investors pulled $US465.3 million from the Ark Innovation fund on Tuesday, according to Refinitiv Lipper data. Morningstar said Tuesday was the fund's biggest daily outflow on record. Out of the last 35 trading days, the fund has seen only five daily outflows and attracted $US5.691 billion in new dollars through February 23.

Bets on companies that have thrived during the pandemic including Tesla, streaming company Roku Inc and payments company Square Inc, have helped the fund's assets swell from $US1.8 billion at the end of 2019 to $US27.6 billion through mid-February of this year, according to Lipper.

Meanwhile, short interest in the fund's shares showed a massive spike, with 100 per cent of the shares available for shorting currently out on loan, FIS Astec Analytics data showed.

Short sellers typically borrow and sell shares they expect to fall in value, hoping to buy them back at a lower price to pay back the loan and pocket the difference. David Lewis of FIS Astec Analytics said his firm's data on borrowing costs suggests potential buying of the ETF as the price falls.

According to Ark Invest's website, the Tesla share purchases were carried out in three instalments worth about $US124 million, $US39 million and $US8 million. On the same day Ark Invest's funds also sold $US126 million of Taiwan Semiconductor's US-listed shares. Ark Invest now holds a more than 0.5 per cent stake in Tesla for a weighting of 6.6 per cent across all its funds. The Ark Innovation fund has large positions in so-called momentum stocks, which tend to attract investors based on thematic trends rather than fundamentals or valuation.

REUTERS

HEADLINE: Payday for Qld flood victims
TEXT:
The Queensland government and state-owned company SunWater have reached a $440 million settlement with 6500 residents affected by the 2011 Brisbane floods.

The settlement, which covers 50 per cent of the liabilities for the damage suffered, comes after long-running legal action against the government.

Several public inquiries cleared dam engineers over the release of water from Brisbane's Wivenhoe Dam, which exacerbated the flooding. But law firm Maurice Blackburn sued the state government and Sunwater for the flood damage in Brisbane's western suburbs.

Thirty-three people died in the 2011 floods, but most of the deaths occurred after flash flooding in Toowoomba and Grantham in the Lockyer Valley on January 10.

Maurice Blackburn principal Rebecca Gilsenan said the $440 million settlement followed a complex and hard-fought legal battle for flood victims.

HEADLINE: Frontbencher accused of rape
TEXT:
The Australian Federal Police and police in two states have been told about historical allegations of rape against a member of cabinet in the federal government.

An anonymous letter shared with Prime Minister Scott Morrison requested urgent action be taken to investigate the alleged rape, said to have occurred in 1988, before the accused person entered politics.

Labor's Senate leader Penny Wong and Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young confirmed on Friday night they had forwarded the letter to AFP Commissioner Reece Kershaw and police in two states.

The letter, first reported by the ABC, included a detailed statement prepared by the complainant.

The woman's story has been known to politicians and journalists in Canberra for some time. She reportedly wrote to then prime minister Malcolm Turnbull in 2019, before taking her own life.

Optional pay rise with 'flexible' super
TEXT:
The Morrison government is considering allowing workers to dip into superannuation for expenses such as housing, or to choose a pay rise over extra super contributions above 9.5 per cent, as part of a "more flexible" retirement savings system.

The potential changes could be used as a trade-off to proceed with the legislated rise in the superannuation guarantee to 12 per cent between July 2021 and 2025.

Ministers also indicated employees such as public servants and university workers who get more than the minimum super guarantee may be able to take the extra amount as take home pay.

In his first significant response to the government's retirement income review, Treasurer Josh Frydenberg on Friday said compulsory super was important, but "more flexibility" in the system would allow people to better balance their working life income and their retirement income.

Mr Frydenberg said the current system provided options for people who wanted to save more for retirement, but was "very limited" for people who wanted to save less to maintain their quality of life today.

"While compulsion will remain an important part of our system, providing Australians with more flexibility should not be seen as an attempt to undermine the system overall. Far from it," he said.

"The earlier Australians interact with the system, the more engaged they will be and the more ownership they will feel over their own savings. More flexibility also means better accommodating the many different circumstances Australians finds themselves over the course of their lives."

The retirement income review found there was a range of lifetime expenses such as housing, healthcare and education that may be more important for people to spend money on in the immediate term, rather than waiting decades to tap into super savings in retirement.

Speaking at a retirement income forum hosted by the Council of the Ageing on Friday, review panel member Deborah Ralston said she liked "flexibility" in super contributions.

"It's really important not to impose on people things that make their life currently harder, but to give them the flexibility when they can afford to save more to save more," Prof Ralston said.

Buoyed by a perceived positive response to its COVID-19 measure which allowed people to withdraw up to $20,000 from super, the government is considering making the measure permanent for home ownership.

Mr Frydenberg said the scheme had allowed people to stay in their homes, keep their kids in school and provide for their families during a challenging period, while still ensuring they had an adequate income in retirement.

"The COVID-19 early release of superannuation scheme was an example of how greater flexibility can benefit those that need it," he said.

The super guarantee is legislated to increase from 9.5 per cent to 12 per cent in 0.5 percentage point increments per year from July 1 through to 2025.

A final decision on whether to proceed with the increase is expected in the May budget.

Grattan Institute economist Brendan Coates said the Treasurer's comments about allowing greater flexibility in the super system were telling, saying letting people cash out any increase in the SG above 9.5 per cent would be "a neat compromise position".

Labor's superannuation spokesman Stephen Jones said the party would oppose moves to broaden the limited reasons people were allowed to dip into super, as well as any move to make the increase in the rate voluntary.

Mr Jones said history and behavioral economics showed when faced with higher take home pay today or a higher retirement income in the future, most people would choose the immediate boost to their future detriment.

"I don't need an economist to tell me," he said. "25-year-old Stephen Jones, if faced with the choice between $10 a week towards retirement savings or $10 a week to enjoy with my mates at the local pub, the pub won out every time."

Labor and the super sector strongly oppose any move to pause or not proceed with the increase, and have targeted the government over the 15.4 per cent rate received by politicians and public servants.

Mr Jones said it was unsustainable for any politician to say 15.4 per cent was fine for them, but 9.5 per cent was adequate for everyone else.

Asked whether the increase could be made voluntary, Superannuation Minister Jane Hume said it was extraordinary how inflexible the system was.

Labelling as "disingenuous" arguments about politicians receiving 15.4 per cent super while limiting others to 9.5 per cent, Senator Hume said she found it "extraordinary limiting" people who received more than the base 9.5 per cent could not choose to take the difference in their pay.

"I think when you talk about things like either withdrawal of super or flexibility of super, surely if the government says this is the legislated rate, that should be the minimum," she said.

"I think it's quite amazing that a negotiation could be made between an employer and whether it be a union or past employees that compels current employees to take the same deal."

Senator Hume also made clear while the government wanted to encourage people to feel safe to draw down on more super in the retirement phase, it would not force them to do so.

The push to encourage greater drawdowns has been the source of significant political tension, with the government and retirement experts on one side, and Labor and parts of the superannuation industry on the other.

Former prime minister Paul Keating last month accused the government of wanting people to die battling to afford their own coffin.

Retirement income review chair Mike Callaghan on Friday said Mr Keating was running a scare campaign and was trading on people's fears and uncertainties to gain a political outcome.
